sources.title: Tomato Diseases: Septoria Leaf Spot (Septoria lycopersici)
sources.claims_supported: Diagnostic circular spots with grey centers and dark margins, rain splash dissemination, survival on solanaceous debris, and cultural sanitation.

sources.organization: Clemson University Cooperative Extension (Home & Garden Information Center)
sources.title: Tomato Diseases & Disorders: Septoria Leaf Spot
sources.claims_supported: Septoria lycopersici fungal pathogen, small circular lesions with dark borders and beige centers, pycnidia fruiting bodies, lower-to-upper canopy defoliation, 68–77°F temperature range, high humidity, 3-year crop rotation, debris removal, avoiding overhead irrigation, and protectant fungicide principles.

safety_and_uncertainty_notes: Presence of tiny black specks (pycnidia) in lesion centers distinguishes Septoria from bacterial spots and early blight. Physical or hand-lens verification is recommended.

causal_agent: Tetranychus urticae (Acari: Tetranychidae / Two-spotted Spider Mite)

symptoms.summary: Fine chlorotic stippling (pale yellow dots) on the upper leaf surface, accompanied by fine silken webbing and a bronzed, dusty appearance on leaf undersides.
foliar_symptoms: Initial damage appears as tiny white or light-yellow speckles/stipples on upper leaf blade
Leaves turn bronzy, yellow, or grayish, become dry and brittle, and drop prematurely
Fine silken webbing covers undersides of leaves and growing shoot tips in heavy infestations
stem_and_fruit_symptoms: Heavy webbing can envelop entire upper foliage clusters; fruit exposed to sunscald; fruit development stunted
look_alike_conditions: Thrips feeding (silvery patches with dark fecal specks)
Tomato russet mite injury (bronze/smoky stems without visible webbing)
Ozone injury

favorable_conditions.environmental_factors: Hot, dry weather (>27°C / 80°F) and low relative humidity; dusty conditions and water-stressed plants exacerbate mite outbreaks
transmission_routes: Wind dispersal on silk threads (ballooning)
Crawling between touching plants; carried on contaminated clothing, tools, and transplants

sanitation: Eliminate weeds along field margins (weeds harbor overwintering mites)
Destroy old crop residue immediately; control dust on roads near fields
irrigation_and_airflow: Maintain adequate irrigation to prevent plant drought stress
Periodic overhead water rinses in small gardens can dislodge mites and raise local humidity
resistant_cultivars: Conserve natural enemies; select tolerant tomato varieties where available

treatment.urgency: Prompt Intervention Recommended: Mite populations reproduce exponentially under hot, dry conditions.
non_chemical_controls: Conserve resident natural predators (such as predatory thrips, ladybird beetles, and minute pirate bugs); in greenhouse structures or where commercially accessible, augmentative releases of predatory mites may be evaluated
Apply botanical extracts such as 5% neem seed kernel extract (NSKE) or registered horticultural oils and insecticidal soaps thoroughly to leaf undersides based on local extension guidance
ipm_chemical_principles: Avoid broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids or organophosphates that destroy predatory mites and cause secondary pest flare-ups
Select selective acaricides / miticides with distinct modes of action (rotate IRAC groups)
safety_and_regulatory_constraints: Mandatory compliance with acaricide product labels, local pest management registrations, worker safety, PPE, REI, and PHI

escalation_triggers: Extensive webbing covering growing tips and upper clusters
Failure of biologicals or approved miticides indicating acaricide resistance

sources.organization: University of California Statewide IPM Program (UC IPM)
sources.title: Pest Notes: Spider Mites
sources.claims_supported: Tetranychus urticae biology, foliar stippling symptoms, web production, hot and dry weather population acceleration, secondary pest flare-ups caused by broad-spectrum pyrethroids/organophosphates, and selective control principles.

sources.organization: University of Florida IFAS Extension (EDIS)
sources.title: Twospotted Spider Mite, Tetranychus urticae Koch (Arachnida: Acari: Tetranychidae)
sources.claims_supported: Pathogen/pest taxonomy, developmental life cycle, chlorotic stippling and bronzing damage, broad host range, predatory insect conservation, and miticide resistance management.

safety_and_uncertainty_notes: Two-spotted spider mites are tiny arachnid pests (0.4 mm), not pathogens. Confirming the presence of moving mites and webbing on the leaf underside with a 10x hand lens prevents misdiagnosis.

symptoms.summary: Small pinpoint lesions expanding into circular to irregular brown spots with pale brown centers and dark brown margins, causing severe defoliation.
foliar_symptoms: Begins on upper or lower leaves as small, water-soaked brown pinpoint spots
Spots enlarge up to 10–12 mm, turning tan to brown with distinct darker brown concentric bands and light brown centers
Leaves turn chlorotic and drop prematurely
stem_and_fruit_symptoms: Elongated brown lesions on stems
Circular, sunken, brown necrotic lesions on fruit, often with cracked or crater-like centers and secondary black fungal growth
look_alike_conditions: Early blight (more distinct circular bullseye rings on older leaves)
Bacterial spot
Septoria leaf spot (smaller with grey centers and pycnidia)

favorable_conditions.environmental_factors: Warm, humid weather (optimally 20°C–28°C) with prolonged leaf wetness (>16 hours) and high relative humidity
transmission_routes: Spores disseminated by wind and splashing water
Overwinters on crop residues and a wide range of alternative weed and crop hosts (cotton, soybean, cucurbits)

sanitation: Remove and destroy infected crop residue immediately post-harvest
Control weed hosts around the perimeter
prevention_and_cultural.crop_rotation: Rotate away from solanaceous and other susceptible host crops for at least 2 years
irrigation_and_airflow: Avoid overhead irrigation; stake and prune plants to improve airflow
Use wider plant spacing to accelerate canopy drying
resistant_cultivars: Select tolerant cultivars where commercially evaluated

treatment.urgency: Monitor and Manage: Preventative fungicide programs are most effective before canopy closure.
non_chemical_controls: Pruning lower canopy leaves to reduce humidity and remove early inoculum
Maintaining balanced plant nutrition
ipm_chemical_principles: Preventative fungicide applications before disease onset or when environmental conditions favor infection
Alternate FRAC mode-of-action classes (e.g. QoI, SDHI, protectants) to delay resistance development
safety_and_regulatory_constraints: Use only pesticides registered for target spot on tomatoes in your region
Strict adherence to label instructions, PPE, REI, and PHI
No proprietary dosage claims

escalation_triggers: Rapid defoliation despite protectant applications
High incidence of fruit lesions in commercial production

sources.organization: University of Florida IFAS Extension (EDIS)
sources.title: Target Spot of Tomato in Florida (Publication PP351)
sources.claims_supported: Corynespora cassiicola causal agent, pinpoint lesions enlarging with concentric rings and yellow chlorosis, distinguishing from bacterial spot and early blight, deeply pitted fruit lesions with cracking, warm wet weather epidemiology, dense canopy moisture retention, and fungicide resistance management.

sources.organization: Purdue University Extension (Vegetable Crops Hotline)
sources.title: New Disease Report – Target Spot of Tomato
sources.claims_supported: Corynespora cassiicola target spot identification, concentric necrotic foliar lesions resembling early blight, 68–82°F temperature and extended leaf wetness triggers, survival in crop debris, crop rotation utility, and canopy pruning/spacing for leaf drying.

safety_and_uncertainty_notes: Target spot lesions closely resemble early blight and bacterial spot. Microscopic examination of conidia is frequently required to distinguish Corynespora from Alternaria.

causal_agent: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV; Begomovirus, family Geminiviridae)

symptoms.summary: Severe plant stunting, erect bushy growth, small cupped leaves with prominent interveinal and marginal chlorosis (yellowing), and heavy flower drop.
foliar_symptoms: Marked upward cupping/curling of leaf margins
Leaf size drastically reduced
Prominent yellowing (chlorosis) along margins and between veins
Leaves become thick, leathery, and brittle
stem_and_fruit_symptoms: Shortened internodes leading to compact, bushy, stunted plants
Flowers drop off without fruit set; fruits formed before infection remain small and unmarketable
look_alike_conditions: Tomato leaf curl New Delhi virus (ToLCNDV)
Physiological leaf roll (leaves roll upward without severe stunting or chlorosis)
Tomato mosaic virus
Herbicide drift

favorable_conditions.environmental_factors: Warm, dry conditions that favor high populations and activity of the insect vector, the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
transmission_routes: Transmitted persistently by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci)
Not seed-transmitted; not mechanically transmitted by sap or tools
Spreads via infected transplants and alternative weed hosts

sanitation: Rogue out and destroy virus-infected plants immediately during early season
Remove alternate weed hosts around fields
prevention_and_cultural.crop_rotation: Rotate with non-host crops and avoid continuous tomato cropping; where coordinated regionally, maintain a host-free period of at least 2 months to break whitefly vector cycles.
irrigation_and_airflow: Protect nurseries with fine insect-proof netting (40–50 mesh nylon screens)
Use reflective silver/aluminum mulches to repel whiteflies
resistant_cultivars: Plant certified TYLCV-resistant hybrids carrying Ty-resistance genes (e.g. Ty-1, Ty-3) which provide strong field protection

treatment.urgency: Urgent Preventive Action (Vector Control): Viruses cannot be cured once the plant is infected; management targets the whitefly vector and sanitation.
non_chemical_controls: Install yellow sticky traps (10–15 traps/ha) for early whitefly population monitoring
Release natural predators (e.g. Encarsia, Eretmocerus, Chrysoperla) in protected greenhouses
ipm_chemical_principles: There are NO chemical cures for plant viruses
Vector management utilizes selective insecticides or systemic drench treatments at transplanting, rotating IRAC groups to prevent whitefly insecticide resistance
safety_and_regulatory_constraints: Never apply chemicals claiming to 'cure' plant viruses
Insecticide use must follow local registrations, label rates, pollinator safety warnings, PPE, REI, and PHI

escalation_triggers: High whitefly infestation levels; widespread viral symptoms across young plantings
Suspected breakdown of resistant cultivars

sources.title: Tomato Diseases: Leaf Curl (Tomato Leaf Curl Virus)
sources.claims_supported: Symptoms of downward rolling/curling, whitefly vector transmission, barrier crops, yellow sticky traps, and rogueing

sources.organization: University of California Statewide IPM Program (UC IPM)
sources.title: Tomato: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl (TYLCV)
sources.claims_supported: Begomovirus taxonomy, Bemisia tabaci vector dynamics, host-free periods, reflective mulches, and resistant varieties

safety_and_uncertainty_notes: No chemical treatment cures a viral infection. Symptoms can mimic abiotic leaf rolling or other viruses; vector management and resistant cultivars are the primary defenses.

symptoms.summary: Mottling of leaves with alternating light green and dark green patches, leaf blistering, distortion, and occasional 'shoestring' narrowing of leaflets.
foliar_symptoms: Characteristic mosaic pattern of light-green and dark-green patches
Leaf puckering, blistering, and distortion
Leaflets may become severely reduced and narrow (shoestring or fern-like appearance)
Plant growth may be moderately stunted
stem_and_fruit_symptoms: Internal browning (brown wall) of fruit tissue
Blotchy ripening
Necrosis or streaking on stems in severe strains
look_alike_conditions: Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV)
Cucumber mosaic virus (CMV)
Tomato yellow leaf curl virus
Herbicide injury (e.g. 2,4-D hormone damage)

favorable_conditions.environmental_factors: Wide temperature tolerance; symptoms most pronounced during periods of rapid vegetative growth in warm weather (20°C–28°C)
transmission_routes: Extremely stable and contagious; transmitted mechanically via sap through contaminated hands, tools, stakes, and plant contact
Seed-borne on the seed coat
Persists in dried crop debris and tobacco products for years; not insect-transmitted

sanitation: Use certified virus-free seed (or soak seed in 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP) or hot water)
Wash hands with soap and water or milk before handling plants; prohibit tobacco use around tomato plantings
Disinfect pruning tools frequently
prevention_and_cultural.crop_rotation: Avoid replanting solanaceous crops immediately in beds with high infested debris
irrigation_and_airflow: Handle plants only when dry
Avoid brushing against plants during cultivation
Rogue out and carefully dispose of infected plants without touching healthy ones
resistant_cultivars: Plant cultivars with TMV/ToMV resistance genes (Tm-1, Tm-2, or Tm-2^2) which offer reliable genetic control

treatment.urgency: Urgent Sanitation Action: There is no chemical cure for viral infections; prompt rogueing prevents mechanical spread to adjacent plants.
non_chemical_controls: Rogue out and safely destroy infected plants immediately upon detection to arrest mechanical transmission

Disinfect pruning knives, shears, and stakes between plants using appropriate sanitizing solutions (e.g. 10% household bleach, 10% trisodium phosphate, or 20% non-fat dry milk where practiced), and wash hands thoroughly with soap and water after handling plants
ipm_chemical_principles: There are NO chemical fungicides, bactericides, or viricides that eliminate ToMV from infected plants
Chemical sprays are completely ineffective and inappropriate against viral agents
safety_and_regulatory_constraints: Do not apply pesticides for mosaic virus management
Strict focus on sanitation, seed health, and genetic resistance

escalation_triggers: Widespread mosaic symptoms in greenhouse or commercial seedling operations
Unexpected infection in known resistant hybrid lines

sources.title: Tomato Diseases: Mosaic (Tomato Mosaic Virus)
sources.claims_supported: Tomato Mosaic Virus causal agent, light and dark green mottling symptoms, leaf distortion, fern leaf / shoestring symptom, mechanical transmission via contaminated tools, clothes, and worker contact, survival in infected crop debris, use of disease-free seed, and rogueing infected plants.

sources.organization: The Ohio State University Extension (High Tunnel Disease Facts)
sources.title: Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV)
sources.claims_supported: ToMV taxonomy and distinction from TMV, worldwide prevalence, mechanical transmission by grafting and contaminated tools/workers, seed-borne transmission, absence of insect vectors, scouting, resistant varieties, and rigorous sanitation of seed, soil, tools, and hands.

safety_and_uncertainty_notes: Viral mosaic cannot be cured with chemical sprays. Symptom expression can vary with cultivar and environmental temperature; laboratory serological (ELISA) testing is required for definitive confirmation.

symptoms.summary: Foliage is vibrant green, vigorous, fully expanded, and completely free from necrotic spots, water-soaking, fungal sporulation, mosaic mottling, or pest stippling.
foliar_symptoms: Characteristic deep green compound leaves with glandular hairs
Healthy leaflet margins without curling, necrotic spotting, or chlorotic halos
stem_and_fruit_symptoms: Stems sturdy, erect, and green without dark streaks or cankers
Flower clusters and green/ripe fruit develop normally without blemishes, rot, or cracking
look_alike_conditions: Latent early-stage infections before symptom expression
Transient minor abiotic stress (e.g. slight temperature fluctuation or temporary drought wilt)

favorable_conditions.environmental_factors: Daytime temperatures 21°C–29°C, nighttime temperatures 15°C–20°C; 60%–70% relative humidity; fertile, well-draining sandy loam or loamy soil with pH 6.0–7.0
transmission_routes: Not applicable (healthy physiological state)

sanitation: Maintain weed-free buffer zones around fields to reduce insect vector reservoirs
Sanitize trellising stakes, pruning knives, and crates
Remove senescent lower foliage
prevention_and_cultural.crop_rotation: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops (cereals, legumes, brassicas) on a 2- to 3-year cycle
irrigation_and_airflow: Use drip irrigation with fertigation to keep foliage dry
Stake, cage, or trellis plants
Maintain row spacing of 60–90 cm for canopy aeration
resistant_cultivars: Utilize certified hybrid seeds with multiple disease resistance traits (e.g. Ty, Mi, Ve, Fol resistances) adapted to local season

non_chemical_controls: Weekly foliar scouting of upper and lower leaf surfaces
Soil test-based balanced fertilization (preventing excess nitrogen and ensuring sufficient calcium and potassium)
ipm_chemical_principles: No chemical fungicides, bactericides, or insecticides are warranted or recommended for healthy foliage
Preserve natural biological control agents and pollinators
safety_and_regulatory_constraints: Unnecessary prophylactic pesticide application causes economic waste, environmental contamination, and risks pest resurgence

escalation_triggers: Poor fruit set, blossom end rot, sudden plant wilting, or root problems despite green foliar appearance
